outcome: Answered in the negative in August 2025 (arXiv:2508.18475, v1 25 Aug 2025): Steininger and Yurkevich exhibit the Noperthedron, a point-symmetric convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, and prove it does not have Rupert's property, so not every convex polyhedron has it. This is the only event I found that bears on the universal question since 26 Jan 2024; it has no journal publication in the sources I could reach, rests on a computer-assisted case analysis, and has two Lean formalizations.
problem_asks: (a) For every convex polyhedron P in three-dimensional Euclidean space (no restriction on size, face count or symmetry). (b) P has Rupert's property, meaning that a hole can be cut through P so that a copy of P, of the same or larger size, can pass through it (Wikipedia's lead definition; the research papers use a straight hole and identical copies). A 'yes' answer needs (b) for all P. A single convex polyhedron without (b) answers 'no'. Nothing else is asked.

events.what_happened: Jakob Steininger and Sergey Yurkevich posted 'A convex polyhedron without Rupert's property' (arXiv:2508.18475; math.MG, cs.CG, math.CO). They construct the Noperthedron, a point-symmetric convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, 240 edges and 152 faces (150 triangles and two regular pentadecagons, per Quanta and Wikipedia), and prove that it does not have Rupert's property (Theorem 1: 'The Noperthedron does not have Rupert's property'). The 2017 question they answer is attributed in the paper to 'the authors of [4]' (identified as Jerrard, Wetzel and Yuan by the Gosain and Grimmer paper, which quotes it as Conjecture 1.1: every convex polyhedron in R3 is Rupert). The same paper also constructs a polyhedron that is Rupert but not 'locally Rupert' (the Ruperthedron, per a search summary). Press: Quanta (Erica Klarreich, 24 Oct 2025); John Baez's Azimuth blog (28 Aug 2025).
events.revisions: v1 25 Aug 2025 (arXiv abs: 'Mon, 25 Aug 2025 20:40:00 UTC'); v2 28 Jan 2026 (current; arXiv abs: 'Wed, 28 Jan 2026 18:50:04 UTC'). Differences found: v1 Lemma 33 lacked an assumption; footnote in v2: 'In a first version of this manuscript we were lacking this assumption and we thank David Renshaw for pointing it out.' v2 acknowledgements thank David Renshaw and Jason Reed for formalizing the paper in Lean and for correcting several inaccuracies of the first version; v1 acknowledgements do not mention Lean. Wikipedia's article notes the disproof (lead, 'until late 2025'). Search summaries gave other version dates (30 Jan 2026, 29 Oct 2025); I used the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Refutes the universal claim: exhibits one convex polyhedron (the Noperthedron) with no Rupert passage, i.e. no straight hole through it admits an identical copy of it (the paper's Definition 3 uses rotations and orthogonal projections with no scaling, so the theorem is about identical copies). Restrictions: the Noperthedron is point-symmetric and the paper's Definition 3 is stated for point-symmetric convex polyhedra; the Lean repository's module structure (Rupert/Equivalences) suggests the paper's characterization is shown equivalent to the general IsRupert, which I did not check. Scope note (my reduction, not stated in the paper): Wikipedia's definition allows same-or-larger copies. If a copy nu*P with nu >= 1 passes through a hole in P, then with P centred at an interior point P is contained in nu*P, so P passes through the same hole. So the identical-copy theorem also gives the same-or-larger negative answer.
events.remains: Nothing of the question remains open once this event is accepted: the universal claim is refuted by one polyhedron. Not addressed by this paper: which other convex polyhedra lack the property. Conjectured non-Rupert solids named in Steininger and Yurkevich's 2023 paper (rhombicosidodecahedron, snub dodecahedron, snub cube, per Gosain and Grimmer's quotation of their Conjecture 3.3) are not settled here; a search summary reports the Noperthedron paper says its methods do not settle the rhombicosidodecahedron (I did not verify this in the paper text).

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (independent formalizations; see events lean-jcreedcmu-noperthedron and lean-dwrensha-rupert). SageMath rational verification of the solution tree (about 30 hours per v1 section 7), with the search tree itself generated by floating-point R code that the paper says is not part of the proof.

events.directly_checkable: The vertices are explicit: orbits of three rational points under a 30-element rotation group (v1 section 1). The polyhedron can therefore be written down. The non-Rupert claim cannot be checked by hand: it rests on a solution tree of 585,200 interior nodes and 18,115,245 leaves (17,492,530 closed by the global theorem and 622,715 by the local theorem; v1 section 7). The leaf checks are rational versions of both theorems, run in SageMath.
events.doubts: (1) v1 lacked an assumption in Lemma 33 (footnote in v2, crediting David Renshaw). Fixed in v2 as far as the sources show; I did not compare the v1 and v2 proofs of Lemma 33 myself. (2) The case analysis is computer-generated: the solution tree was generated with floating-point R code, and rigour depends on the rational verification in SageMath and the Lean checks. (3) A later paper still treats the question as open and does not cite this paper: Gosain and Grimmer, arXiv:2509.08190 (v1 9 Sep 2025, about two weeks after v1 of this paper), states Conjecture 1.1 ('every convex polyhedron in R3 is Rupert') and says it 'remains open whether every polyhedron in three dimensions is Rupert'. No text or bibliography mention of the Noperthedron appears in their v1 full text as fetched.
events.direction: Negative. The problem asks whether every convex polyhedron has the property; this paper exhibits a convex polyhedron that does not. It answers the 'every' in the negative and says nothing about polyhedra other than the Noperthedron.
events.object: The Noperthedron: a point-symmetric convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, 240 edges and 152 faces. Its vertices are explicit (orbits of three rational points under a 30-element rotation group). What it shows: no straight hole through it admits an identical copy of it (Theorem 1). The construction is explicit; the non-existence of passages is shown by a computer-assisted exhaustive case split over the 18,115,245 leaves of a search tree, checked in exact arithmetic (SageMath) and formalized in Lean.

events.what_happened: Tony Zeng, 'A stellated tetrahedron that is probably not Rupert' (arXiv:2604.26531; math.MG, cs.CG, math.CO). Proposes searching for the simplest non-Rupert convex polyhedron; defines a convex polyhedron as the convex hull of a finite set of points in convex position. Studies the stellated tetrahedron P11/20 (convex by construction; Figure 3 caption: 'We conjecture this convex polyhedron to not be Rupert'). Reports no Rupert passage for 88% of an encoding of SO(3) x SO(3) under the standard measure, using linear programming (the paper uses an LP solver and the shapely package). States 'Nevertheless, we conjecture that this stellated tetrahedron is not Rupert.' The abstract says the work 'provide[s] numerical evidence'. Cites Steininger and Yurkevich as having 'recently constructed a convex polyhedron which is not Rupert'.
events.delivers: Numerical evidence and a conjecture that one specific convex polyhedron, P11/20, is not Rupert. Not a proof: the paper says it has no local theory and so cannot show the full non-Rupert claim. If established, it would be a second convex polyhedron without the property; it would not change the Noperthedron result.
events.remains: Whether P11/20 has the property is open on this paper's account. The universal question is already answered negatively by the Noperthedron, so this event bears only on the status of P11/20.
events.time_since_posted: about 5.5 months (as of 11 Oct 2026); no engagement found in my searches
events.directly_checkable: The polyhedron is defined by its vertex set (a stellated tetrahedron as a convex hull); the 88% figure comes from an LP computation over a parametrized family of orientations, not from a closed argument.
events.doubts: The paper calls its result numerical evidence; the title says 'probably'; the 88% figure leaves about 12% of the encoded orientations unaccounted for in the text I read; the paper says it lacks a local theory.
events.direction: Would cut against the universal claim if established. As written it is a conjecture supported by numerical evidence.
events.object: P11/20, a stellated tetrahedron presented as a convex polyhedron (convex hull of its vertices). The paper claims numerically that for about 88% of an encoded parameter space of orientations there is no Rupert passage; the claim that P11/20 is not Rupert is conjectural.

events.what_happened: Ivo Fagundes David de Oliveira, Tanya Khovanova and Yogev Shpilman, 'Lonely Solids' (arXiv; v1 submitted 18 Jun 2026; math.HO; MSC 52A15, 00A08). Two convex solids are friends if each can pass through a suitable hole in the other; a solid is lonely if it has no friends, including itself. Results: a convex solid is lonely iff it has constant width; every non-constant-width convex solid has a simple friend (an arbitrarily long, arbitrarily thin rectangular cuboid); any two such solids are connected by a chain of at most three handshakes. The paper cites the Noperthedron as Rupert-failing ('the noperthedron is not a friend of itself') and the Noperthedron paper as bibliography [5].
events.delivers: A characterization of friendship among convex solids. On my reading of the definitions, a constant-width convex solid has no self-friendship and so lacks the Rupert property; the paper does not present constant-width polyhedra, and I did not verify whether any convex polyhedron has constant width. The paper does not address whether every convex polyhedron is Rupert.
events.remains: The universal question for polyhedra is untouched by this paper.
events.time_since_posted: about 4 months (as of 11 Oct 2026); I did not run a search specific to this paper's reception
events.direction: Neighbouring. It uses the Noperthedron as a non-self-friendly example and characterizes a different relation. It does not cut the polyhedral question.

events.what_happened: Kavin Satheeskumar and Liam Benoit, 'On Nieuwland Numbers and Polar Duality' (arXiv:2608.14912; math.MG; MSC 52B10). The Nieuwland number of P is the largest nu with nu*P passing through P. Abstract: they reduce passage of P through Q to a feasibility problem over a quadratic constraint set; prove that the Nieuwland number of the octahedron is 3 sqrt(2)/4; and show the Nieuwland number of a convex polytope can be computed by polynomially many semialgebraic optimization problems in a fixed number of variables. Theorem 10 gives a dual-passage condition; Theorem 14 gives equality of the cube and octahedron Nieuwland numbers; Theorem 18 is the polynomial-time algorithm. The bibliography cites the Noperthedron paper as [10] and the 2023 Steininger–Yurkevich Math. Comput. paper as [9].
events.delivers: Nieuwland number of the octahedron = 3 sqrt(2)/4 (equal to the cube's), via a duality argument, plus a polynomial-time algorithm for Nieuwland numbers of convex 3-polytopes. Concerns the largest passing scale, not whether every convex polyhedron has the property (the octahedron is already known to be Rupert).
events.time_since_posted: about 2 months (as of 11 Oct 2026); not searched for reception
events.direction: Neighbouring. It settles a passage-scale constant for the octahedron, not the existence question for all convex polyhedra.

events.what_happened: Raj Gosain and Benjamin Grimmer, 'Some New Insights from Highly Optimized Polyhedral Passages' (arXiv:2509.08190; math.OC, math.MG; v1 only, 9 Sep 2025). summary: The question was answered negatively in August 2025. Steininger and Yurkevich (arXiv:2508.18475, v1 25 Aug 2025, v2 28 Jan 2026) construct the Noperthedron, a point-symmetric convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, and prove that it does not have Rupert's property (Theorem 1). Wikipedia's lead and Quanta (24 Oct 2025) report the same, and the Wikipedia article was revised 29 Sep 2026. The result is inside the window and is the only event I found that bears on the universal claim. Its support is computational: a solution tree of 18,115,245 leaves, generated in floating-point R and checked in exact arithmetic in SageMath (about 30 hours). Two Lean 4 projects formalize it (jcreedcmu/Noperthedron, whose files I read contain no sorry and whose main theorem depends on a ValidTable input that the README says is checked from a shipped table; and dwrensha/Rupert.lean, whose Nopert #214 file I did not open). Human engagement is thin: the only documented gap was in v1 Lemma 33, found by David Renshaw and fixed in v2, which acknowledges Renshaw and Jason Reed for the Lean formalization. Quanta and Baez report the result and quote reactions but do not say anyone checked the proof. I found no journal publication. The AI search (OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic, Gemini, Claude, AlphaEvolve and tracker queries) found no AI involvement in this result: the paper's acknowledgements name no system, and neither Lean repository mentions AI. The only AI statement among the related papers is in the Steininger–Yurkevich octahedron paper (9 Sep 2026). It credits Gemini Flash 3.7 with help on Figure 1 and TikZ graphics, and Claude Fable 5 with fixing typos and pointing out inaccuracies in an early version, and says 'All ideas in this work and its write-up are human'. I did not put these in ai.systems because the involvement stopped at figures and proofreading, and the paper concerns the octahedron's Nieuwland number, not this question. Other events: Zeng (29 Apr 2026) gives numerical evidence and a conjecture that the stellated tetrahedron P11/20 is not Rupert, with no proof; Gosain and Grimmer (9 Sep 2025) still describe the question as open and do not cite the Noperthedron; Lonely Solids (18 Jun 2026) and Satheeskumar–Benoit (14 Aug 2026) cite the Noperthedron. Satheeskumar–Benoit prove the octahedron's Nieuwland number is 3 sqrt(2)/4 and the octahedron paper proves the same; these concern passage scale for a polyhedron already known to be Rupert. Scope: the paper's Definition 3 uses identical copies and no scaling, while Wikipedia says 'same or larger'. My reduction is that a larger passing copy yields an identical passage through the same hole when the copy is centred on an interior point, so the identical-copy theorem also gives the negative answer for Wikipedia's definition. The paper states Definition 3 only for point-symmetric polyhedra, which the Noperthedron is. The 2023 Steininger–Yurkevich paper and the 2017 Jerrard–Wetzel–Yuan source are reached through snippets or the citing paper's text; I did not open them. A Murphy lead about a 'nopert' snub cube is unverified; I found no completed proof.
competing_reading: A strict standard of 'settled' would count this as claimed rather than settled. The argument is computer-assisted, has one revised gap (v1 Lemma 33), has no journal publication, and its formal checks are partial (I did not inspect IsRupert, the table module, or Nopert #214). Against that: the formal checks, the revision history and the rational SageMath verification together make a refutation by a single explicit polyhedron hard to dispute. On scope, a reader using the strict-increase convention of the Nieuwland papers (nu > 1) would still get a negative answer, because the absence of identical passages implies the absence of larger ones.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A journal publication, or a written human verification of the 18-million-leaf case analysis. (2) Confirmation that the Lean IsRupert definition matches the paper's identical-copy definition, and that MainTheorem builds its ValidTable in-kernel from the shipped table. (3) The Nopert #214 file in dwrensha/Rupert.lean, checked for sorry. (4) The full v2 text, sections 8 and 9 and the bibliography, which I did not reach. (5) Whether the rhombicosidodecahedron, snub dodecahedron or snub cube are settled later, which would matter only for further counterexamples.

event.what_happened: Jakob Steininger and Sergey Yurkevich posted 'A convex polyhedron without Rupert's property' (arXiv:2508.18475; math.MG, cs.CG, math.CO). They construct the Noperthedron, a point-symmetric convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, 240 edges and 152 faces (150 triangles and two regular pentadecagons, per Quanta and Wikipedia), and prove that it does not have Rupert's property (Theorem 1: 'The Noperthedron does not have Rupert's property'). The 2017 question they answer is attributed in the paper to 'the authors of [4]' (identified as Jerrard, Wetzel and Yuan by the Gosain and Grimmer paper, which quotes it as Conjecture 1.1: every convex polyhedron in R3 is Rupert). The same paper also constructs a polyhedron that is Rupert but not 'locally Rupert' (the Ruperthedron, per a search summary). Press: Quanta (Erica Klarreich, 24 Oct 2025); John Baez's Azimuth blog (28 Aug 2025).
event.revisions: v1 25 Aug 2025 (arXiv abs: 'Mon, 25 Aug 2025 20:40:00 UTC'); v2 28 Jan 2026 (current; arXiv abs: 'Wed, 28 Jan 2026 18:50:04 UTC'). Differences found: v1 Lemma 33 lacked an assumption; footnote in v2: 'In a first version of this manuscript we were lacking this assumption and we thank David Renshaw for pointing it out.' v2 acknowledgements thank David Renshaw and Jason Reed for formalizing the paper in Lean and for correcting several inaccuracies of the first version; v1 acknowledgements do not mention Lean. Wikipedia's article notes the disproof (lead, 'until late 2025'). Search summaries gave other version dates (30 Jan 2026, 29 Oct 2025); I used the arXiv abstract page.
event.delivers: Refutes the universal claim: exhibits one convex polyhedron (the Noperthedron) with no Rupert passage, i.e. no straight hole through it admits an identical copy of it (the paper's Definition 3 uses rotations and orthogonal projections with no scaling, so the theorem is about identical copies). Restrictions: the Noperthedron is point-symmetric and the paper's Definition 3 is stated for point-symmetric convex polyhedra; the Lean repository's module structure (Rupert/Equivalences) suggests the paper's characterization is shown equivalent to the general IsRupert, which I did not check. Scope note (my reduction, not stated in the paper): Wikipedia's definition allows same-or-larger copies. If a copy nu*P with nu >= 1 passes through a hole in P, then with P centred at an interior point P is contained in nu*P, so P passes through the same hole. So the identical-copy theorem also gives the same-or-larger negative answer.
event.remains: Nothing of the question remains open once this event is accepted: the universal claim is refuted by one polyhedron. Not addressed by this paper: which other convex polyhedra lack the property. Conjectured non-Rupert solids named in Steininger and Yurkevich's 2023 paper (rhombicosidodecahedron, snub dodecahedron, snub cube, per Gosain and Grimmer's quotation of their Conjecture 3.3) are not settled here; a search summary reports the Noperthedron paper says its methods do not settle the rhombicosidodecahedron (I did not verify this in the paper text).

event.time_since_posted: 13.5 months since v1 (25 Aug 2025) and 8.5 months since v2 (28 Jan 2026), as of 11 Oct 2026. No journal publication found; the arXiv abstract page lists no journal reference. Public reactions found (Baez blog; Quanta quotes from Joseph O'Rourke and Benjamin Grimmer) are reactions, not checks: none of them says they worked through the proof. O'Rourke: 'The natural conjecture has been proved false.' Grimmer describes running his own search on the rhombicosidodecahedron.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (independent formalizations; see events lean-jcreedcmu-noperthedron and lean-dwrensha-rupert). SageMath rational verification of the solution tree (about 30 hours per v1 section 7), with the search tree itself generated by floating-point R code that the paper says is not part of the proof.

event.directly_checkable: The vertices are explicit: orbits of three rational points under a 30-element rotation group (v1 section 1). The polyhedron can therefore be written down. The non-Rupert claim cannot be checked by hand: it rests on a solution tree of 585,200 interior nodes and 18,115,245 leaves (17,492,530 closed by the global theorem and 622,715 by the local theorem; v1 section 7). The leaf checks are rational versions of both theorems, run in SageMath.
event.doubts: (1) v1 lacked an assumption in Lemma 33 (footnote in v2, crediting David Renshaw). Fixed in v2 as far as the sources show; I did not compare the v1 and v2 proofs of Lemma 33 myself. (2) The case analysis is computer-generated: the solution tree was generated with floating-point R code, and rigour depends on the rational verification in SageMath and the Lean checks. (3) A later paper still treats the question as open and does not cite this paper: Gosain and Grimmer, arXiv:2509.08190 (v1 9 Sep 2025, about two weeks after v1 of this paper), states Conjecture 1.1 ('every convex polyhedron in R3 is Rupert') and says it 'remains open whether every polyhedron in three dimensions is Rupert'. No text or bibliography mention of the Noperthedron appears in their v1 full text as fetched.
event.direction: Negative. The problem asks whether every convex polyhedron has the property; this paper exhibits a convex polyhedron that does not. It answers the 'every' in the negative and says nothing about polyhedra other than the Noperthedron.
event.object: The Noperthedron: a point-symmetric convex polyhedron with 90 vertices, 240 edges and 152 faces. Its vertices are explicit (orbits of three rational points under a 30-element rotation group). What it shows: no straight hole through it admits an identical copy of it (Theorem 1). The construction is explicit; the non-existence of passages is shown by a computer-assisted exhaustive case split over the 18,115,245 leaves of a search tree, checked in exact arithmetic (SageMath) and formalized in Lean.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether every convex polyhedron is Rupert; one explicit convex polyhedron without the property answers it in full, so the Noperthedron paper is scope whole, direction refuted, object a counterexample. The record's reduction from same-or-larger copies to identical copies is sound, so the definitional mismatch does not narrow scope. Verification was the close call. A Lean build alone would be unreviewed (F7), but David Renshaw is named in the paper as having formalised it with Jason Reed. In doing so Renshaw found and corrected a missing assumption in Lemma 33, which is a human working through the argument in public view, so I answered digested (F9). Gosain–Grimmer's silence two weeks after v1 is too soon to count as a doubt. The Lean repositories formalise known work (none, date unplaceable). Zeng offers only a conjecture with numerical evidence (none). The Nieuwland-number and lonely-solids papers answer different questions (variant). The octahedron paper's AI use was figures and typo/inaccuracy checking only, so ai none. Pre-snapshot events are positive instances, except that Scott's sufficient conditions settle a class (case).
judgement.doubts: Renshaw's qualification is not established in the record, and the digestion rests on the paper's acknowledgement rather than a statement by Renshaw himself; a stricter reader would answer unreviewed, giving claimed rather than resolved. The 18-million-leaf computation has not been checked by a human, and the record did not confirm that the Lean IsRupert definition matches the paper's definition.
